projectBackground.name: Retail Demand Reporting
projectBackground.timeline: Report due before Monday's trading meeting
projectBackground.context: The weekly revenue report shows a 20% jump nobody can explain. You suspect the SQL behind it.

manager.name: Anouk Visser
manager.note: A query that runs is not a query that's right. Check the row counts before you trust the totals.

assignment.title: Find why revenue is inflated
assignment.brief: Reason about joins and row counts, find the cause of the inflated total and explain the fix.

documents.name: Customers Table
documents.note: 3 customers: C1 has 2 orders, C2 has 3 orders, C3 has none.

documents.name: Orders Table
documents.note: Each order has one customer_id; order_items link to orders.

documents.name: Weekly Revenue Query
documents.note: Joins customers, orders and order_items then sums order total.

tasks.title: Which Join?
tasks.prompt: You need every customer, including those with no orders. Which join do you use from customers to orders?
options: RIGHT JOIN from orders to customers without checking
tasks.reasoning: A LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table even without matches.
tasks.tip: Choose the join by which table must keep all its rows.
tasks.mistake: INNER JOIN silently drops customers with no orders.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Row Count After Left Join
tasks.prompt: C1 has 2 orders, C2 has 3 and C3 has none. How many rows does customers LEFT JOIN orders return?
tasks.reasoning: Each matching order creates a row; a customer without orders still yields one row with NULLs.
tasks.tip: Predict row counts before running the query.
tasks.mistake: Counting only orders (5) forgets the unmatched customer.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Customers Without Orders
tasks.prompt: Which pattern finds customers with no orders?
options: INNER JOIN and WHERE orders.id IS NULL
LEFT JOIN orders and WHERE orders.id IS NULL
tasks.reasoning: After a left join, unmatched rows have NULL in the right table.
tasks.tip: IS NULL on a right-table key identifies non-matches.
tasks.mistake: An inner join cannot return unmatched rows.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: WHERE vs HAVING
tasks.prompt: You want customers whose total spend is above 500. Where does the condition go?
tasks.reasoning: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
tasks.mistake: Using WHERE with an aggregate raises an error or filters the wrong thing.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Why Revenue Is Inflated
tasks.prompt: Select likely causes of an inflated revenue total after joining orders to order_items.
options: Duplicate rows from a one-to-many join
Summing a header-level value at line level
Order total repeated once per item row
tasks.reasoning: Joining a header to line items repeats header values; summing them multiplies revenue.
tasks.mistake: Summing header fields at line level is the classic fan-out error.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Explain the Fix
tasks.prompt: In 3-4 sentences explain why revenue was inflated and how to correct the query.
tasks.modelAnswer: The query joined orders to order_items and then summed the order total, so each order's total was repeated for every item row, inflating revenue. To fix it, sum the line-level amount (quantity x price) from order_items, or aggregate order totals in a subquery before joining. I would verify by comparing the new total with the order table total and checking row counts at each join.
tasks.reasoning: A good explanation names the grain problem, gives the fix and a validation step.
tasks.tip: Fix, then verify with a reconciliation.
tasks.mistake: Changing the query without reconciling leaves the risk unproven.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

caseStudy.title: Case Study: The 20% Jump That Wasn't
caseStudy.background: A dashboard showed 20% revenue growth for a week. Finance later found a join fan-out; true growth was 3%. Marketing had already increased spend.
caseStudy.challenges: No one compared dashboard totals to the finance ledger.
questions: How did the join cause inflated totals?
What check would have caught it?
caseStudy.solution: Helix added a reconciliation test to every revenue report comparing totals with the finance system.
caseStudy.lessonsLearned: Reconcile every report to a trusted source before sharing.
